articles.text: Prosecuting attorney Long, of Morton county, in an interview published in the Mandan Pioneer, again rakes Judge Francis fore and aft. It behooves the judge to deny some of the charges, or resign immediately. We are loath to believe, however, that Francis is as unscrupulous as is claimed and shall give him the benefit of the doubt until he is proven guilty.
articles.summary: Packard notes Prosecuting Attorney Long's renewed attack on Judge Francis in the Mandan Pioneer and urges the judge to answer or resign.

articles.text: We are glad to see that the Stockgrowers' Journal is also willing to state the exact facts in reference to the cow business. If there are any losses, or any unprofitable points come up, we believe that the plain facts should be given to the public. Nothing can be gained by concealment, for the truth is bound to come out at last. The cattle business is undoubtedly the most profitable legitimate business in the world and why some editors wish to "paint the lily" by magnifying its profits, is beyond our comprehension.
articles.summary: Editorial agreeing with the Stockgrowers' Journal that the plain facts of the cattle business should be published.

articles.text: The cattle are by this time nearly out of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations in Indian Territory. As long as the authorities at Washington are satisfied that cattlemen in these sections are acting in good faith, no penalty will be inflicted on account of the forty-day limit being stretched. An official telegram received at Washington Tuesday stated that there are about 25,000 cattle on the reservations now and that they will be removed within thirty days.
articles.summary: Cattle are nearly cleared from the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservations in Indian Territory.

articles.text: Suits and counter suits have arisen over the cattle trail troubles and the end unless delayed too long or finally allowed to die a natural death, will be interesting. Messers Blocker, Campbell Pugsley, Donahoe & Fleming, Bennett & West Bros. Webber, C. A. Pugsley, Ringo Williams & Brown, Dowling, Vaughn Carrigan, Creswell, J. W. Driskill, Davis Childers and Pryor Bros. have all been indicted for driving Texas cattle, infected with Texas fever, into the Indian Territory and through the imbroved herds in northern part of the Territory. The first six men and firms mentioned above have brought counter-suits for causing the stoppage of their cattle in Indian Territory for an aggregate amount of $317,500.
articles.summary: Texas trail drivers indicted for bringing fever-infected cattle into Indian Territory have filed counter-suits totaling $317,500.

articles.text: It is now finally decided that the boundary line between Montana and Dakota was located twelve miles too far east. It then behooves the advocates of an honest county organization to get out their pencils and figure some more. The additional twelve miles of railroad will bring the taxes from that source up to if not quite $5,500. This will pay the ordinary running expenses of a county organization. In addition, we are credibly informed that Stark county's assessment will be about $4,000. This makes over $9,000, to which must be added the $1,400 we are now paying Morton county for liquor licenses. The whole makes a total of far more than enough to pay the expenses of a county organization. In addition to all this is to be added over $200,000 of taxable property that the changing of the line brings into Billings Co., and we ask any friend of the law, of the common good, of his own pocket book, shall we organize? The answer, taking into consideration everything, must be an almost unanimous affirmative.
articles.summary: With the Montana-Dakota line found to be twelve miles too far east, Packard argues the added tax base makes organizing Billings County affordable.

articles.text: The prairie fires on the west extend from Beach to Sentinel Butte and thence south of the track for at least ten miles and it may go fifty before it stops. A movement ought certainly to be made to find the parties responsible for the fire and punish them to the full extent of the law.
articles.summary: Prairie fires west of Medora stretch from Beach to Sentinel Butte and south of the track.

articles.text: The long waiting is finally over and Marquis de Mores is a free man. When the case was given to the jury it took them less than ten minutes to come to a verdict of acquittal. The Marquis is to be congratulated on the result and every true friend of the west will rejoice in his acquittal. There is no one man in Dakota who has done more to develop the west than he, and a conviction in his case would have been a calamity to western Dakota. The merits and demerits of the affair are now set at rest and it would do no good to bring them all to mind. To any who are disposed to cast blame on the Marquis for the killing of Luffsey, we would say, put yourself in his place. Virtually a stranger in a strange land, almost entirely unacquainted with the habits and entiely so with the people, is it strange that he should have adopted fatal measures to protect his life which no one will say he did not believe was in danger? The fact that his life was probably in no real danger has nothing to do with his belief. Any one, situated as he was, would come to the same conclusion. The expenses of the trial hsve been very heavy, but it is probably better that the matter is now finally set at rest.
articles.summary: Packard celebrates the jury's acquittal of the Marquis de Mores in the Luffsey killing, reached in under ten minutes.

The Chicago market shows very little change from our last week's report. In only one class, stockers, is there a change of over 10c. The receipts at Chicago last week were 41,000 head, against 36,000 the week before. Two-thirds of the arrivals were Texan and Western cattle. There were but few well-matured beeves, they bringing fully previous prices, while the commoner grades averaged 10c. lower. Montana and Dakota range cattle sold as high as $5; Dakota Texans up to $4.25 and Nebraska and Wyoming Texans averaged $3.25. A train-load of 1,265 lb Montana cattle sold at $5 and some extra fine Texans brought $4. The market is steady, with an upward tendency. The Liverpool and New York markets were also a trifle higher.
articles.summary: Chicago cattle quotations and market report; Montana and Dakota range cattle sold as high as $5.

articles.text: The Little Missouri Horse Co. received a valuable addition to its herd last week. They received a car-load of blooded horses from Pennsylvania, of which the following is a list. One three-year-old stallion, half French coach horse and half Norman, one yearling Norman stallion, three sucking Norman colts and eleven French coach, Norman and standard bred trotting brood mares. The consignment arrived in first-class shape, under the charge of B. Speers, who will break some horses at the Co's. ranch this fall. Messrs. articles.summary: The Little Missouri Horse Co. received a car-load of blooded Pennsylvania horses.

articles.text: The air has been full of smoke from prairie fires for the last week and from all sides, especially the east, come accounts of serious loss. We think at a moderate estimate, 100,000 bushels of wheat and oats have been burned, besides houses, agricultural implements, etc. It seems that in most cases, not even the most ordinary precautions have been taken to guard against fire. An ordinary double furrow, will stop a prairie fire nine times out of ten. Two double furrows, fifteen or twenty feet apart, with the grass burned between, will stop any prairie fire that ever existed. Such criminal carelessness as allowing a wheat or oat stack to remain in a stubble field or prairie, without such a simple and effective protection as a furrow or two, is hard to explain. The recent losses will prove a serious but instructive lesson to the grangers.
articles.summary: Smoke from prairie fires has filled the air for a week; Packard estimates 100,000 bushels of grain burned and urges fire furrows.

articles.text:
During their recent beef round-up, the Bad Lands cattle Co. branded the following stock:
Seven Maltese cross calves,
Six Elkhorn calves and eleven Elkhorn yearlings,
Four VI calves,
One SOHO calf,
One TD (on side) calf,
One 76 (monogram) bar calf,
One KC F calf,
One B [brand with bar beneath?] [calf?] and
Three quarter circle diamond calves.

The above action inaugurates a new movement among our cowmen and one that we hope to see gonerally followed hereafter. It gives cattle owners a feeling of greater confidence to know that others are also looking after their interests. It will also join the members of the Association together more firmly for the common good and cultivate a feeling of confidence in each other that is now too often lacking. We suggest that other outfits following this plan, send their lists to the Cow Boy for publication also.
articles.summary: During its beef round-up the Bad Lands Cattle Co. branded strays of other outfits, including Maltese cross and Elkhorn calves, and published the list.

articles.text: Measers, Small, of Glendive, and DuVal, a stock holder in the LeMoyne cattle Co., were here Monday. It has been decided not to remove the L C herd this fall and on account of the overstocking of the North Yellowstone ranges we consider it likely that they will range where they are at present or somewhere else in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Small of Glendive and DuVal of the LeMoyne Cattle Co. visited; the LC herd will not be moved this fall.

articles.text: Over 50,000 cattle have been driven this season to the ranges north of the Yellowstone and already they are becoming so crowded that several outfits are looking for new locations.
articles.summary: Ranges north of the Yellowstone are crowded after 50,000 cattle were driven in this season.

articles.headline: How to Take off a Hide.
articles.text: The hides of farm-slaughtered animals have a poor reputation, because of the careless way in which they are stripped. Calf skins and sheep-pelts are reduced one-half in value by being cut and gashed, and improperly stretched. When a hide is stripped off, it should be stretched at once, and pegged out to dry, with the flesh side upward. If it is rolled up, or thrown into a heap and left to dry in that shape, it is so mean-looking that a buyer will offer only half its real value. A few hints in regard to taking off a hide, may be useful. The throat should never be slit cross-wise, either in killing or taking off a hide. The skin is slit from the chin down the brisket, in a straight line to the tail; it is then cut around each hoof; the hind legs are slit behind over the gambrel, but the fore legs are slit up in front, over the knees. This leaves the skin in good shape for finishing the leather. The head and legs are first carefully skinned, and all cutting of the skin is avoided. The skin is then easily drawn off by taking hold of it firmly, and pulling it steadily. It is then spread out evenly on a floor, and salted with fine salt. If there is but one, it is best to take it out as soon as the salt has taken, and dry at once in a cool, shaded place. If there are more than one, they are laid upon each other and salted quite freely, and afterward are thoroughly dried. If the skins are to be kept on hand, they should be closely watched for moths or grubs.--[Montana L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted advice from the Montana Live Stock Journal on skinning and curing hides.

articles.text:
If the "Dakota Blizzard" of Casselton, would consolidate with the "weekly Ozone," of Steele, and the "BAD LANDS COW BOY," of Medora, with the "Dakota Siftings," of Minnewaukan, what a team they would make. Just think of it! The daily "Ozone Blizzard," what a dose that would be. And worse still, the daily "Cow Boy-Siftings," or rather the "Cow Boy Sifter," for the cow boys are said to be fond of making "sifters" of all obstinate people who don't agree with them. There is no accounting for newspaper men's taste for startling and gorgeous names.--[Jamestown Capital.

We readily admit that the name of our paper has a sensational side but we did not originate it with that end in view at all. There is really no more appropriate name for a paper in the world than the BAD LANDS COW BOY. The first part designates the place of publication, in the heart of the Bad Lands; the second certainly carries the true impression, that it deals mainly in cattle news. Editors are requested to look at this side of the mirror in the future.
articles.summary: Packard reprints the Jamestown Capital's joke about Dakota newspaper names and defends the name Bad Lands Cow Boy.

articles.headline: A Lawyer Jailed by a Judge.
articles.text:
At the trial of the Marquis de Mores [at?] Bismarck, a remarkable incident occurred which illustrates the hostile feeling existing between Judge Francis and some of the members of the bar. A correspondent says: Several witnesses had been examined. Irvine Kinley and Frank Pecket testified to having heard Luffsey and companions threaten De Mores' life. Justice Mark Bateman testified concerning the examination in his court and his discharge of De Mores on the ground that Luffsey was killed in self-defense and when resisting arrest. Howard Eaton testified that he was sent by De Mores to meet Sheriff Harmon, warn him that the Luffsey party would resist arrest, and advise him that De Mores and party would prevent their leaving town. Thomas Carruthers, who was with De Mores' party but some distance away from the place where the firing began, testified that he saw smoke from the first shots, and they were fired by Luffsey and companions. Martin Wadsworth testified regarding O'Donnel's quarrel with De Mores. This witness had been dismissed, when Prosecuting Attorney Long of Mandan called him to his side, and privately asked him if he was the Wadsworth who had accompanied Wannegan to visit De Mores in jail. Being answered yes, Long then asked to be permitted to place Wadsworth again on the stand. Objection was made, and the court ruled that the witness could not be placed on the stand again unless he was called as a witness for the prosecution.

Long undertook to state what he intended to prove, and was called to order, and ordered to take his seat, but continued speaking, when the judge vigorously used his gavel, and threatened to commit him for contempt. In the course of his remarks Long advanced close to the judge, and gesturing with his right hand near to the judge's face, said:

He came here unwillingly to perform official duty. He had no feeling in the case. He only desired to see a fair and impartial trial. He appeared as a subordinate officer of the court, and was here to assist in the enforcement of substantial justice; that instead of the court extending to him the aid and support which he was entitled under the law to expect, the court had uniformly, during the whole trial, sought to tie the hands of the prosecution and openly aided the defense; that the court had shown by its action in this case that it had determined to aid in the acquittal of the defendant, and that the court would not leave a stone unturned in the accomplishment of such acquittal; that the court throughout had shown a most marked feeling in favor of the defendant and against the prosecution; that the court had sought at every point to embarrass the prosecution and to aid in the acquittal of the defendant.

During all this time and for some time after, while Long was still talking, Judge Francis endeavored to silence him by the use of the gavel and by threats to commit him for contempt, but Long dared the judge to commit him and talked himself out, when the judge ordered him in custody, and he was taken to the jail building. The court then took a recess to 2 p. m.

During the recess dinner was sent to Long from the Sheridan house with a message to the effect that an apology for his conduct would be accepted and it need not be abject, but he must expect the court to preserve its dignity at all hazards. In jail Long said to a correspondent:

I have done nothing to regret. I have only tried to perform an official duty, and in the performance of that Judge Francis has abused me personally and insulted me repeatedly professionally. I shall stay here until I am ordered out. I will ask no favors or concession, and will grant none. I have no apology to make, and will make none. I maintain that Judge Francis acted in a manner unbecoming the office of a judge, and provoked me to say all that was said.

When the court opened at 2 p. m., Long was brought in and refused to apologize.
articles.summary: Wire report from the De Mores murder trial at Bismarck: witnesses described Luffsey's threats, and Judge Francis jailed Prosecuting Attorney Long for contempt.

articles.summary: Leonard and Warren Phillips of Boston are visiting Howard Eaton to hunt.

articles.summary: Jim Harmon was thrown by a broncho and hurt.

articles.text: Remember when you have any insurance policies you want made out, that it is always better to have it done by a home agent who will personally look after your interest. The Cow Boy office is the place to get your insuring done.
articles.summary: Notice that insurance can be had at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Osborne Bros. Æ brand appears in to-day's issue. Their range is on Andrew's creek, north of Sentinel Butte. Their herd, at present, is not very large, but as they will use Angus bulls, the quality of their herd will soon be unsurpassed on the river. We will have something to say in the future about this herd, as we believe that Polled Angus and Galloway grades are to be the northwestern range cattle of the future.
articles.summary: Osborne Bros.' Æ brand ad appears; they will use Angus bulls on their Andrew's creek range.

articles.text: H. B. Wadsworth, while superintending the Bad Lands cattle Co's. shipment of beeves at Dickinson, last Saturday, slipped and fell from the top of a caboose, breaking his leg in the fall. Mrs. M. Wadsworth went to Dickinson, to attend him. The accident will disarrange Mr. Wadsworth's business plans and it is to be hoped that he will speedily recover.
articles.summary: H. B. Wadsworth broke his leg falling from a caboose while shipping Bad Lands Cattle Co. beeves at Dickinson.

articles.text: One by one they join the Benedicts, and now it is Maxwell's turn to get ready to fight if anyone says he hasn't the best wife in the world. Mrs. Josie Maxwell, nee Smith, is the happy bride and all join in the hope that the newly married couple may experience none but the joys of life in their new relation of husband and wife. They return to-night and will go immediately to housekeeping in the cottage formerly occupied by Dr. Jorgens.
articles.summary: Maxwell has married Josie Smith; the couple return tonight to the cottage formerly occupied by Dr. Jorgens.

articles.text: Word came in yesterday that E. G. Paddock was discharged on his trial for complicity in the Luffsey killing. Prosecuting attorney Long turned the case over to Judge Francis, who probably discharged him on the same evidence that acquitted the Marquis. This will probably set the whole matter at rest, as, even if Moore and Miller are tried they must be acquitted.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock was discharged on the charge of complicity in the Luffsey killing.
